238.t: Nat King Cole's big band rehearses at her house
238.s: Lloyd Wilson brought Nat Cole's band to rehearse and jam at her home; she recalls Nat's show, wife Nadine and brother Eddie.
238.q: That's right. Well, Lloyd Wilson would bring -- he'd go up to Central Avenue, which was just -- you know, as I said, we lived just a block from the avenue, and he would go and bring these guys. Well, Nat King Cole, for instance. I've certainly got to mention that. He brought Nat, he brought Nat…

238.t: Jam sessions at her house with Lloyd Wilson
238.s: Lloyd Wilson brought visiting musicians to her home near Central Avenue, where Eddie Barefield, Panama Francis and Benny Carter jammed.
238.q: was a little premature baby, so -- and we used to -- we lived not far from -- still in that same neighborhood. It was so wonderful that I managed to live and stay in that same neighborhood all this time, until 1947, you know, when I started recording. Then I moved to the west side. But all this…

238.t: Who played at the jam sessions at her house
238.s: She names Eddie Cole, Panama Francis, Al Morgan, Lloyd Wilson, Forest Powell and Marshall Royal among those at her house sessions.
238.q: I can't remember, frankly. The only person, I think, that I can remember, was his brother Eddie, who was at that time a bass player, and Eddie of course has gone on also. Eddie later got with a group, he had a group, I can't remember what they called themselves, but he had an entertaining group,…

88.t: Sunday jam sessions at the Trouville
88.s: Each Sunday the Nat Cole trio and Lee backed tenor, alto and trumpet players in sessions that Lee says Los Angeles started.
88.ch: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
88.q: But now the Trouville was where they had the best sessions - jam sessions - they ever had in Los Angeles. What we used to do at the Trouville -- the rhythm section was always Nat; you know, the trio and myself, most of the time. That was then, like, one Sunday, we had Lester, Ben, Bumps, and I…

88.t: Sunday jam sessions at Billy Berg's and the $500 union fine
88.s: Lee ran jam sessions, was fined $500 after one that brought in players from the Ellington and Lunceford bands, and lived next to the Union.
88.ch: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
88.q: You know? There was a band on recording, so anyway -- they heard about us back east. But to tell you more about Billy Berg's, I used to give jam sessions there every Sunday. Now, I would call the musicians. What would happen, well -- I was fined once $500 because in Los Angeles, they did not want…

166.t: Byas and other tenor players at Los Angeles jam sessions
166.s: He recalls Byas, Andy Anderson, Bob Darcy and pianists at LA jam sessions.
166.ch: Los Angeles in 1935: school, jam sessions and the hobo trip west
166.q: He wasn't working with anyone. He was just -- had blown everyone away, jam sessions. There was two tenor players here. One would see how loud he could play, and the other one would see how much he could play, you know. But both of them were good tenor players. And Andy Anderson was more in the…

166.t: Jam sessions at Nellie Lutcher's house, and Don Byas wiping everyone out
166.s: Players gathered at Nellie Lutcher's; Byas made everyone play every tune in every key.
166.ch: Clarifications and portraits: Lester Young, Byas, Blanton, Ben Webster
166.q: Uh-huh. We just jammed everywhere we could find to jam -- that's you know -- oh, most favorite spot to jam was around Nellie Lutchers house.

90.t: Sunday sessions with Hampton Hawes and Wardell Gray
90.s: Sunday jam sessions with Hawes, Sonny Criss, Wardell Gray and other session regulars.
90.ch: Los Angeles: Roy Milton and Central Avenue
90.q: In the meantime, Hampton Hawes, the pianist, he was coming out of high school just about the time that Sonny was coming out of school. So we all would play on Sundays out there. And Wardell Gray had moved out here, and we would play out there... We had some fantastic sessions out there on Sunday.…

90.s: Slim Gaillard at the Toddle House, and Sunday sessions where he met Warne Marsh, Clifford Solomon and Hadley Caliman.
90.q: [LAUGHS] Slim Gaillard was doing some work out at the Toddle(?) House out in Culver City, not only after that; he was out there at the Toddle(?) House and broadcasting from the kitchen, broadcasting recipes in different languages. [LAUGHS] Yeah, that was beautiful.

664.s: He names the regulars at his house sessions, which grew too big, including Coco, Bill Walde and Stanley Maddison.
664.ch: Back to the horn: house sessions
664.q: I don't either...well we had Coco and all them guys used to come out there...Coco the guitar player...we had Bill the bass player...we had Stanley Maddelson...used to come out there...the piano player...

230.t: Apex Club, Alabam and a Watts church jam session
230.s: Barnet recalls the Dunbar Hotel clubs in Los Angeles, Freddie Green's drumming, and an all-night jam session in a Watts church with Hampton, Covey, Purvis and Bumps Meyers.
230.q: Oh, golly, I don't know. I remember there was a drummer by the name of Freddie Green, who did everything that Lionel did, you know. I think he'd been watching him pretty closely, and throwing the sticks around, and I remember he was in one of the bands. But I couldn't tell you the name of the…

87.t: After-hours jamming in Los Angeles and T-Bone Walker
87.s: On Lunceford trips he, Willie Smith and Joe Thomas jammed at a club out in the fields, where T-Bone Walker worked and Ben Webster showed up (mostly inaudible).
87.q: Yeah, this was way back when I was with Lunceford, and there was open way out by, out that way, called Honey's, and There wasn't nothing but open fields out there at that time. But T-Bone Walker used to go out there in fact, he was working out there, and I always liked the way he'd sing the blues.…

28.t: After-hours jam sessions with Ainkion, Oscar Ellman and Bill Coleman
28.s: After work musicians jammed: the Czech saxophonist Ainkion, Alix Combelle, an unnamed trombonist, Bill Coleman, and Argentine guitarist Oscar Ellman; King George loved jazz and asked to hear it.
28.ch: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
28.q: Now, when we would get finished, we'd have jam sessions. And there was a fellow named Ainkion (phonetic), very handsome fellow. He was a Czechoslovakian. He could play a lot of saxaphone. He could play a lot of saxaphone and he had another boy named Alex Campbell. He could play a lot of tenor…

233.t: A New Year's Eve jam session with Batman and Carl Perkins
233.s: Anthony Ortega took Monk to a Los Angeles house party jam where Carl Perkins played and Monk, with chops up, asked to sit in.
233.ch: Leaving Hampton: Europe and Los Angeles
233.q: : It was associated with it, right. I went to a jam session on...It was Christmas, during the holiday, New Year's. Anthony Ortega, he was also in the band. I forgot about him. We called him "Batman." Batman was in the band, and he lived in Los Angeles. And when I got there, well naturally, he was…

94.s: Moore describes houses turned into joints, jamming with Art Tatum, and how lively Los Angeles was.
94.q: Oh, yes! I mean, oh --every, every house seems to be a huge joint, you know. The joints sprung up. And at that time I remember playing with Art Tat m. At the jam session I get my horn out, and I hear -- every time I see Art I used to get my horn out and play. And, those sessions were all, all…

412.t: Running Village jam sessions in a loft, 1943-44
412.s: After the radio, Hodes ran jam sessions in a Village loft at a dollar a head. He lists the players he had.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: But he objected. So I lost the job. But in that time, I gained an audience, and I started running jam sessions in the Village. And we found a place that was just perfect for us. Seats that would slant up. And -- yes, theater type of thing, but it was actually a loft. And the -- a dollar apiece to…

235.t: The Cecil Hotel and nightly jam sessions in New York
235.s: Musicians stayed at the hotel, and every night Don Byas, Lester Young, Dizzy, Eddie Davis and others jammed downstairs.
235.q: : Well anybody would be subject to be staying there, you know. It's whoever was in town. But, you know, you could eat there...you could eat downstairs, they

454.t: Jam sessions in California: Charlie Christian and the Whitman Brothers
454.s: He was refused a seat next to Charlie Christian; Joe Comfort's electric bass and Maxwell Davis's playing.
454.ch: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
454.q: Those were the days, man. It's no fun no more. There's a couple of guys that have got a studio in the village, they call themselves -- they have a jam session and they're making noise. Everybody's doing what they want to do.

168.t: Hour-long jam sessions, stamina and cheating on fast tempos
168.s: They played one tune like I've Got Rhythm for an hour, with Nat Cole and Lee Young; Stewart now sometimes plays in two to save his arm.
168.ch: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
168.q: Oh, yes, we would play sometimes two and three choruses on different things. We'd play and -- and I can remember playing even one number, 'I've Got Rhythm,' for maybe about an hour or so.

169.t: Jack's Basket and the Los Angeles jam scene
169.s: Jack's was the main jam spot with Wardell and Dexter dueling.
169.ch: Erroll Garner and the Los Angeles scene
169.q: That was the joint where the real heavy swing Jazz was being played. You know, Wardell and Dexter used to tie up every night practically. And Wardell was playing, too, man. He was playing some horn, man. But Dexter was in there, too. He was fighting right there with him.

97.t: White musicians jamming uptown after hours
97.s: Benny Goodman, Harry James and others come up to jam and borrow riffs.
97.q: there was Mexico's, Pod's and Jerry's, private houses in the basement there, they used to have a piano. Now, you could go in there and buy a drink, because it didn't cost nothing then, and sit down, and you could play if you wanted. Piano players would come in -- those white fellows -- Benny…
